facts.text: Hope was a female blue whale. She stranded on a sandbar at the mouth of Wexford Harbour, Ireland, on the morning of 25 March 1891.
The whale was not yet fully grown when she stranded.
facts.note: Do not call her a juvenile or a calf: the NHM pages say she was about 15 years old.

facts.text: The 4.5-tonne skeleton was sold to the Natural History Museum for £250.
The skeleton hung in the museum's Mammal Hall from 1934.
The skeleton was moved to Hintze Hall and unveiled there in July 2017.
In Hintze Hall she replaced the cast of Dippy the Diplodocus, which stood there from 1979 until January 2017.
She was named Hope "as a symbol of humanity's power to shape a sustainable future".

unsourced_facts.text: The skeleton has 221 bones and is posed in a diving lunge.

shots.narration: My skeleton is twenty-five point two metres long. And I wasn't yet fully grown.
shots.action: Tiny visitors stand frozen on staircase and floor, looking up; at 1.5s the skull's empty eye socket blinks open into a bright cartoon eye that swivels to camera. Then She shakes her head hard, cables twanging, and grins at camera, talking. Then Hope, free of the bare skeleton behind, surges the hall's length, tail beating hard, flipper skimming over frozen visitors on the staircase; cables swing in her wake; she brakes hard and hovers, looking back.

shots.narration: My youth wasn't enough to escape the shallows. I'm the only blue whale skeleton in a diving lunge.
shots.action: Hope hovers above the staircase, looks down at frozen tiny visitors, eyes softening, flippers drooping as she speaks, then her tail snaps once, hard. Then Hope rockets to the glazed roof, flips, plunges full speed into the hanging bones, jaw thrown open, throat pleats ballooning; cables swing hard; a deep thud as it locks. Then The skeleton hangs whole and still, jaws angled down; one cable still trembles and a last shimmer of blue fades along the lower jaw.
